comparison: Both evaluate temporal genetic effects (C18-C20, C53). OpenEval finds the delta-R²g methodology sound with validated replication. Peer reviewers question the approach, suggesting alternative methods (interaction terms), and note only 30% validation rate (146/541), finding the evidence unconvincing.

Both address causal modeling (C64-C66). OpenEval finds the permutation-based causal framework methodologically sound with appropriate extensions. Peer reviewers explicitly reject causality claims, stating QQ plot enrichment (C25) shows correlation not causation, and that the indirect residual-based approach is insufficient—direct causal models are needed.

Both evaluate statistical methods for longitudinal data (C60-C61). OpenEval supports the repeated measures approach as appropriate. Peer reviewers question optimality, suggesting interaction terms would be more efficient than simple time point comparisons.

Both assess methodological advantages of the longitudinal design (C28-C30, C77). OpenEval finds empirical support for enhanced genetic effect detection. Peer reviewers acknowledge the design as 'innovative' but raise substantial concerns about sex confounding, suboptimal statistical choices, weak causality evidence, and low validation rates that undermine efficiency claims.

Both evaluate study design and cohort structure (C11-C12, C38-C39). OpenEval finds the sex-stratified design with clear criteria rigorous. Peer reviewers raise critical concern that discovery (males only) and replication (females only) confound sex with cohort, questioning whether findings are robust or sex-confounded.

Both address limitations regarding causality (C33, C80). OpenEval notes appropriate acknowledgment that sample size is insufficient for causal inference. Peer reviewers strongly agree, emphasizing that causality is not well demonstrated and validating the authors' recognition of this limitation.

Both evaluate the 20-gene identification and pathway enrichment (C15-C16, C21, C24). OpenEval finds strong evidence from integrative analysis across cohorts. Peer reviewers did not challenge the gene identification or functional enrichment results themselves, focusing concerns on methods and causality interpretation rather than these findings.

Both address correlation analyses and gene counts (C22-C23). OpenEval finds appropriate statistical thresholds and validation. Peer reviewers did not dispute these descriptive findings about gene numbers and correlations, though they questioned analytical methods and causality interpretation.

Both evaluate study limitations and design rationale (C31-C32, C79). OpenEval finds honest acknowledgment of constraints. Peer reviewers did not challenge these design choices (ethnic homogeneity, age restrictions) or limitation acknowledgments, focusing concerns elsewhere.

Both address pathway enrichment findings (C21, C24). OpenEval finds convergent evidence from multiple tools. Peer reviewers did not challenge the pathway enrichment results, which are included in their supported gene identification evaluation.

OpenEval evaluates overall study design including array platforms (C47, C86) as rigorous with appropriate quality control. Peer reviewers specifically requested clarification on how different Illumina array versions (HT-12v3 vs v4) were combined and how normalization was performed across time points and cohorts, indicating uncertainty about data integration procedures.

OpenEval finds Q-Q plot deviation (C25) supports enrichment of true associations in the integrative analysis. Peer reviewers explicitly state that QQ plot enrichment does not provide evidence of causality, only correlation, challenging the interpretation of this evidence.

OpenEval evaluates translational claims about biomarkers and therapeutic interventions (C27, C71-C73, C76, C78) as speculative and requiring validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these future application claims.
OpenEval evaluates background literature and context claims (C1-C10, C54, C67-C69, C74, C82-C84) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval evaluates quality control procedures and bioinformatic methods (C57-C59, C63) as standard and appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical QC claims.
